claims.text: The starting material is a homogeneous, single-phase solid-solution alloy containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 atomic percent each.
Partially replacing a mid-sized constituent with an element having a substantially different atomic radius will increase local atomic-size mismatch.
Increased atomic-size mismatch will enhance local lattice distortions.
The induced lattice distortions will alter specific phonon modes.
The phonon-mode changes caused by lattice distortion will increase electron–phonon coupling strength.
Stronger electron–phonon coupling will produce a higher superconducting transition temperature.
The modified alloy will have a measurably higher superconducting transition temperature than the baseline alloy.
The proposed relationship applies only when the substitution does not cause phase segregation, secondary-phase formation, or an ordering transition.
X-ray diffraction or related structural probes can be used to assess whether the compared alloys remain single-phase.
Electrical resistivity or magnetic susceptibility measurements at cryogenic temperatures can be used to determine the superconducting transition temperature.

Failure of the modified alloy to show a statistically significant increase in transition temperature or a detectable change in phonon-related signatures under identical conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
